item.title: Through a Serbian lens, a different China unfolds in Hainan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
by Xinhua writers Zhang Xuan, Nemanja Cabric BELGRADE, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- On brightly lit Qilou Old Street, vendors slice open pink wax apples, their juice sparkling under the lights. A drone captures traffic weaving across Haikou's cross-sea bridge, while elsewhere, women in ethnic attire craft traditional goods amid lush rainforests, and rockets launch into space from the vast coastline. These vivid scenes unfolded at a documentary screening held in September at the China Cultural Center in Belgrade, where audiences followed Serbian producer Bosko Kozarski and his crew on their journey through Hainan, a tropical island province in southern China. For Kozarski, the trip marked his second visit to China after filming a documentary in Beijing last year. As his China documentary series expands, his own connection with the country is also entering a new chapter. "In Hainan, I experienced a completely different China," Kozarski told Xinhua. While Beijing showcased a grand blend of historical heritage and modern technology, he said Hainan offered him a unique mix of natural scenery, traditional folk customs and modern resort facilities. He described the island in three words: lush, futuristic and hospitable. He attributed "lush" to its tropical landscapes and vibrant vegetation, "futuristic" to its modern architecture and high-quality infrastructure, and "hospitable" to the sincere smiles of locals who make visitors feel at home. Over more than 10 days, the crew traveled across Hainan, including Wenchang, Qionghai, Lingshui, Wuzhishan, Baoting and Changjiang before returning to Haikou. Local guide Huang Zhimin accompanied them. He appeared on camera multiple times under the name "Mason." A native of Wuzhishan in southern Hainan whose ancestors were longtime laborers in Hainan's agricultural development, Huang guided the crew through historical sites, local cuisine and natural landscapes, and even accompanied them on test rides in autonomous vehicles. Huang noted Kozarski and his team's deep fascination with the culture of the Li ethnic group. "They were very interested in Li brocade and traditional dwellings, so I introduced them to the history, customs and intangible heritage in English, and took them to taste Li snacks and sweet wine," Huang said. Kozarski found a strong sense of familiarity in the 3,000-year-old Li textile traditions. Drawing parallels with Serbia's own long-standing weaving heritage, he said this shared "cultural gene" created a cross-regional resonance. Despite the thousands of miles between them, "the cultural language conveyed by the looms is interconnected," he said. But the cultural connections Kozarski discovered were only one part of what Hainan has to offer. His trip also gave him a firsthand look at the island's growing openness to the outside world. As the Hainan Free Trade Port launched its island-wide special customs operations in late 2025, the province has increasingly welcomed international tourists with direct flights, diverse payment methods and advanced transport. Kozarski described his trip as exceptionally smooth, thanks to China's visa-free entry policy, transport networks and digital payments linked to international credit cards. He observed that Hainan is becoming an open global hub for trade and international tourism, facilitating the flow of people, goods and capital and serving as a "smart gateway" to the world. For Serbian audiences, the documentary offered another perspective on China and left a lasting impression on Serbian Marina Milicevic. "China has almost everything a country can possess -- breathtaking natural scenery, well-planned cities, a clean environment, a safe society, and rich, diverse cultures and traditions," she said. Comparing old photographs of Chinese cities with their present-day urban landscapes, she said she was amazed by the transformation. The story of cultural exchanges between China and Serbia is far from over. While guide Huang hopes Hainan's expanded openness will bring more visitors and prosperity, Kozarski is already planning his next trip to China. For Milicevic, the documentary has opened a window onto a China she hopes to explore in person. "Traveling all over China" is now part of her future plans.■

item.title: Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade unveils medals, torch
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Staff members display uniforms and equipment at the 100-day countdown event for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Oct. 7, 2026. The medals, torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled on Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event held at the Changchun International Aviation Expo City. (Xinhua/Xu Chang) CHANGCHUN, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Medals, the torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event at Changchun International Aviation Expo City. The torch, named "Ji Xiang," or "Auspicious Flight," is inspired by the clivia, Changchun's city flower. Its upper section features a filmstrip motif and 12 winter sports icons representing the Games' disciplines, a reference to Changchun's film industry. Snowflake and ginseng flower motifs appear near the top, while ski-inspired lines run down the sides and a wheel-hub pattern decorates the base. The torch stands 711 millimeters tall, a reference to the highest elevation in Changchun's urban area, 711 meters. The medals, named "Ji Meng," or "Auspicious Dream," combine traditional Chinese cultural elements, winter sports imagery and features associated with Changchun. The front features patterns inspired by skate blades and ski tracks, while the reverse depicts the "First Jade Bird of Ancient China," an artifact unearthed at the Wutaishan historic site in Nong'an, Changchun. Part of the bird design is inlaid with Songhua stone from Jilin. A filmstrip pattern along the medal's edge also references Changchun's film heritage. An embedded NFC chip allows athletes to access images of their medal ceremonies and seasonal scenery from Changchun by tapping the medal with a smartphone. Uniforms for torchbearers, torch escorts, volunteers, staff, technical delegates and ceremony personnel were also unveiled. The Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade will be held from January 15 to 25, with competitions in Changchun and nearby Jilin City. ■ The torch is unveiled at the 100-day countdown event for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Oct. 7, 2026. item.title: Russian tourism industry eyes attracting more Chinese visitors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
MOSCOW, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- During China's week-long National Day holiday this year, Chinese tourists are frequently seen on the streets of Moscow. "Russia is a unique country and a must-visit," said Wang Xinzuo, who visited several Russian cities and described his trip as smooth and enjoyable. In the first half of 2026, Chinese tourists accounted for over 50 percent of all inbound tourist trips to Russia. "We are witnessing a substantial rise in travel volumes. In 2025, the number of mutual tourist visits exceeded 3 million. According to our data, 154,200 Chinese tourists visited Russia in the first quarter alone this year, marking a 44 percent increase year on year," Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui said before the holiday. Russia is preparing for further growth. In early September, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko said the country aims to accommodate more than 5.5 million Chinese tourists by 2030. Behind the figures lies an industry adapting to a new generation of Chinese travelers. MOSCOW: FROM GROUP TO INDEPENDENT TRAVEL Moscow remains the main gateway for Chinese tourists. According to the Border Service of the Russian Federation, 240,000 Chinese tourists visited Moscow in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year on year. But the profile of visitors is changing. Guided group tours are becoming less dominant as younger and more independent Chinese travelers arrive. More than 80 percent of travelers from China come to Moscow independently, including for business, according to Bulat Nurmukhanov, deputy chairman of the Moscow Tourism Committee. In response, a China Friendly certification program is expanding in Moscow, covering services such as Chinese-language information, adapted menus and trained staff. The Cosmos Hotel Group told Xinhua that two of its four- and five-star hotels in Moscow have received the certification, with more properties planned to join the program. Moscow has also strengthened its promotion in China through Chinese-language tourism services, social media and cooperation with Chinese travel platforms, while highlighting its cultural heritage and modern attractions. REGIONS SEEK NEW OPPORTUNITIES Beyond Moscow, Russian regions are increasingly competing for Chinese tourists. In St. Petersburg, the number of Chinese tourists has risen by nearly 60 percent since 2021, according to Nana Gvichiya, deputy chair of the city's Tourism Development Committee. Chinese visitors are showing a growing interest not only in historical sites but also in local cuisine and creative spaces. In the Altai region, the number of Chinese tourists increased 1.5 times in 2025 from the previous year, exceeding 6,000 for the first time, said Alexander Baryshnikov, head of the regional Department for Tourism and Resort Development. Although the region receives fewer Chinese visitors than Moscow and St. Petersburg partly because of a lack of direct flights, local businesses are improving services and developing China-friendly tourism products. Several hotels and resorts have received China Friendly certification, while tour operators have developed specialized routes and promoted them through international exhibitions and Chinese social media. In Russia's Far East, the Amur region has recorded a 60 percent increase in Chinese tourists since the introduction of the visa-free policy between China and Russia in 2025, Governor Vasily Orlov said. The region plans more than 200 joint events with China in 2026. A planned cross-border cable car linking Blagoveshchensk and Heihe is also expected to boost tourism. Once completed, the journey between the two countries will take just over two minutes, with an annual capacity of 2.5 million passengers. ADAPTING SERVICES The rapid growth has also exposed gaps in Russia's tourism infrastructure. Experts and tourists cite language barriers, difficulties with digital payments and a shortage of qualified staff, particularly outside major tourist destinations. "Special attention should be paid to the training of professional guides for Chinese groups in Russia," said Anastasia Pavlova, an expert on cultural and tourism cooperation at the Russian State University for the Humanities. Ilya Umansky, president of the Russian Union of Tourism Industry, stressed the need for closer cooperation between the two sides in the tourism sector. "Today we find ourselves in a unique state of revival of our mutual tourist exchanges," Umansky said. "I am confident that we have a great future."■

item.title: Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 7, 2026. Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Wednesday. (Xinhua/Lyu You) STOCKHOLM, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Wednesday. According to the Academy, some molecules, such as amino acids, exist in two variants that are mirror images of each other. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror-image forms. How such chemical asymmetry, known as homochirality, could emerge had long remained a mystery to chemists. "This year's prize recognises discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality," the Academy said in a statement, noting that the two laureates "made chemistry choose a mirror image." "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," says Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry. Kagan, born in France on Dec. 15, 1930, is affiliated with Universite Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, born in Japan in 1950, is a professor at Tokyo University of Science. ■ The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 7, 2026. Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Wednesday. (Xinhua/Lyu You)

item.title: Another Nanjing Massacre survivor dies, only 20 remain
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
NANJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- One more survivor of the Nanjing Massacre passed away on Wednesday, reducing the number of registered living survivors to 20, the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders said. Massacre survivor Guo Xiulan died at the age of 94, according to the memorial hall in Nanjing, the capital of east China's Jiangsu Province. Guo was born in 1932. According to survivor recollections documented by the museum, when the Nanjing Massacre took place after Japanese troops captured Nanjing on Dec. 13, 1937, Guo's parents took their three children to hide in an underground shelter along with neighbors. "Japanese soldiers stood at the opening and strafed it with machine guns. My parents and my youngest sister perished. Only my second sister and I survived," Guo was recorded as saying. The Nanjing Massacre unfolded over six weeks. Japanese soldiers killed approximately 300,000 Chinese civilians and unarmed soldiers in one of the most barbaric atrocities of World War II. Over the years, the number of survivors able to share firsthand accounts of the massacre has continued to decline. In 2014, China's top legislature designated Dec. 13 as the national memorial day for the victims of the Nanjing Massacre. The Chinese government has also preserved survivors' testimonies through written records and video recordings. Documents related to the massacre were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2015. To date, only 20 living survivors of the Nanjing Massacre remain on the registry maintained by the Nanjing Association for Assistance to Victims of Japanese Aggression and Inheritance of Nanjing Massacre Historical Memory. ■

item.title: Culture-infused tourism gains traction during National Day holiday
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- On the morning of Oct. 1, the first day of China's National Day holiday, the Confucius cruise ship slowly pulled away from a port in Jining, east China's Shandong Province, setting off for Nanyang ancient town on the city's southern outskirts. Named after the famous ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius, the ship was bound for a 2-hour-plus journey, passing stretches of the Grand Canal, the world's oldest artificial waterway system, which connects rivers in northern and eastern China and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014. "We chose the cruise after seeing online that it offered a rich cultural experience," said Zhao Xiaojie from the provincial capital Jinan, as she and her 11-year-old son read the ancient texts on the cabin's decorations inspired by the Six Arts -- the six foundational disciplines of ancient Confucian education. Her choice reflects a broader trend during this year's National Day holiday, as cultural content is weighing more and more heavily in China's tourism products. NATIONAL DAY EXTRAVAGANZA "Cruises have operated on the same route before, but the Confucius incorporates many cultural elements and intangible cultural heritage experiences, turning it into a moving showcase of Confucianism on the Grand Canal," said Zhang Feng, head of the cruise route. The round-trip ticket includes shuttle services to scenic spots and admission to the Kangqian Bieyuan and Huji Qianzhuang attractions. Visitors can also watch a traditional fishermen's wedding ceremony and cormorant fishing performances in Nanyang ancient town, Zhang said. Such packages bring together Confucianism and the culture of the Grand Canal, he added. The unusual holiday calendar this year, with the Mid-Autumn Festival falling just three working days before the National Day holiday, has given fresh momentum to the integration of culture and tourism. Data from Chinese online travel platform Ctrip showed that one in 10 travelers chose to combine the two holidays by taking three days off to create a 13-day break. Nearly half of those taking an extended break traveled for more than eight days. The longer holidays have expanded the travel radius of Chinese tourists, bringing cultural and tourism products in more remote and lesser-known destinations into the spotlight. In Cangyuan Wa Autonomous County, southwest China's Yunnan Province, for example, tourists gathered at a square to pound freshly harvested rice and prepare new rice, filling the air with its aroma. "New rice festival activities and service facilities have been upgraded this year, allowing visitors to experience the authentic culture of the Wa ethnic group," said Li Lei, deputy general manager of the Cangyuan County Tourism Investment Company. Traditional culture is not the only draw. A growing number of travelers are also visiting landmarks associated with China's revolutionary history, driven in part by the patriotic sentiment associated with the National Day holiday. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which lasted from 1934 to 1936. The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution. In Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province, the Memorial Park of the Starting Point of the Central Red Army's Long March has attracted large numbers of study-tour groups and is expected to receive nearly 300,000 visits during the seven-day holiday. Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said the flow of visitors to revolutionary landmarks reflects people's emotional identification with the revolutionary traditions. When they travel, they don't just want to see history; they also want to draw deeper inspiration from the revolutionary legacy for their lives today, according to him. INNOVATION REMAINS KEY The trend has also fallen in line with a series of development plans China released recently. The 15th Five-Year Plan for culture and tourism development, released by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism in September, calls for deeper integration between culture and tourism and their mutually reinforcing development with other areas of the economy and society. It stresses supporting the development of distinctive cultural industries and tourism in former revolutionary base areas. Moreover, it calls for expanding the space for cultural and tourism development, with deeper integration moving from resource consolidation and product integration toward new business models and broader applications. Hong'an Township in Xiushan Tujia and Miao Autonomous County, southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, has put such innovation into practice, drawing 190,000 tourist visits in the first two days of the holiday. Leveraging the cultural appeal of Border Town, a novel by renowned Chinese writer Shen Congwen, as well as its unique location where three provincial-level regions meet, the township has developed immersive, scenario-based tourism offerings that combine folk experiences, local cuisine and the nighttime economy. In Shandong, seven cities have joined forces to combine seven popular online-literature IPs with the region's landscapes and historical sites, encouraging fans to turn fictional worlds into real-life travel destinations. The model uses storytelling familiar to Generation Z to breathe new life into traditional cultural and tourism resources, converting online popularity into real-world tourism consumption. "The route runs from west to east, so fans can take a high-speed train and visit a different 'chapter' every day, which is very convenient," said Liu Wei, a fan of online literature born in the 2000s. For industry insiders, such efforts to generate more immersive cultural tourist activities are also necessary. Wu Liyun, a professor at Beijing International Studies University, said scenic spots once relied mainly on ticket sales, which is often unsustainable today. "The core of the industry transformation lies in adding more experiential offerings and opportunities for secondary consumption, with the focus on everyday settings, local culture and lifestyle-oriented services," she said. GLOBAL DRAW The shift has appealed to inbound travelers as well. With China offering unilateral visa-free entry to citizens of 50 countries and full mutual visa exemptions with 29 countries, its tourism industry has also been working to offer overseas tourists a wider range of immersive trips centered on cultural experiences. In Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province, where the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in July, growing numbers of overseas visitors are exploring historic sites, taking part in art workshops and browsing handicraft markets, while enjoying distinctive cafes and homestays. The city, known as the "Porcelain Capital," now offers a range of experiences for visitors seeking to explore its centuries-old ceramic traditions, according to Zhang Chen, a local tourism industry insider. Options include a one-day program combining an introduction to local ceramic culture with hands-on pottery making, or a three-day workshop led by inheritors of intangible cultural heritage. "Many overseas visitors now seek a deeper cultural connection, rather than simply sightseeing," Zhang said. In Beijing, veteran tourist guide Dou Junjie feels a similar trend. He provides guided bicycle tours along the Beijing Central Axis, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2024 that covers former imperial palaces and sacrificial structures. "More overseas visitors to Beijing would like to experience local life and learn about local culture," Dou said. According to Gao Zhengyang, a guest researcher with Jiangsu Su Merchants Bank, immersive travel across destinations is replacing sightseeing and photo stops, a wider range of trendy Chinese products is making its way onto tourists' shopping lists, and the mix of visitors is becoming more diverse. Gao said all of these trends point to improvements in the quality of "China Travel." Data from Ctrip shows that bookings for one-day tours by inbound tourists during this year's National Day holiday and the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday surged by over 400 percent year on year, with scenic spot ticket sales up more than 220 percent and train tickets more than 170 percent. Li Xinjian, a professor at the Beijing International Studies University, said the growth in inbound tourism during what is traditionally a peak season for domestic travel reflects the increasingly diverse experiences on offer. "Overseas tourists are finding that China offers not only beautiful scenery but also engaging cultural experiences," he said. For Wu Liyun, value-added services such as the cultural experiences in Jingdezhen and Beijing are particularly important, as they are far more appealing than standardized products and usually leave a much deeper impression on travelers. Wu believes Jingdezhen's model can be replicated in terms of how cultural content is presented. She cited her hometown of Linyi in Shandong Province, where willow weaving products are widely exported, and tourists can try their hand at the traditional craft and take their own creations home. "Every city has its own ways of life passed down through generations," she said. "What you are accustomed to in the place where you live can be incredibly fresh and novel to outsiders." ■

item.title: China's railways see holiday return peak amid vibrant tourism market
item.description:

(Photo by Du Penghui/Xinhua) BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's railways saw the peak of the holiday return rush on Wednesday, with 24.15 million passenger trips expected on the final day of the National Day holiday, amid strong travel demand and vibrant tourism activity across the country. A total of 2,449 additional passenger trains were scheduled on Wednesday to cope with the surge in demand, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. On Tuesday, the country's railways handled 21.6 million passenger trips, marking the third consecutive day with more than 20 million journeys. Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an, Wuhan, Hangzhou, Chongqing and Shanghai were among the busiest cities for departures and arrivals, while passenger flows were particularly heavy on routes including Beijing-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shenzhen and Xi'an-Chengdu. Railway authorities across the country added services and expanded overnight operations to facilitate the return rush as China's tourism market remained vibrant during the seven-day holiday, with county-level destinations and nighttime consumption emerging as notable trends. County-level destinations gained popularity as travelers increasingly sought slower-paced and more immersive experiences away from major cities. From the coastal county of Lingshui in south China's Hainan Province to Mohe, a county-level city on the country's northern frontier, smaller destinations are drawing visitors with distinctive local experiences. Meanwhile, nighttime consumption flourished in many cities, with cultural performances, night markets, light shows and food fairs extending visitor stays and enriching holiday experiences. ■ Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station in east China's Shanghai, Oct. 7, 2026. item.title: Small counties, big appeal: China's "golden week" fuels diverse getaways
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
*During this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips, averaging 300 million a day. *Cultural and tourism authorities nationwide have introduced a range of creative initiatives to attract visitors, drawing on sports events, cultural IPs, ethnic traditions and distinctive natural landscapes. *On Sept. 24, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China. BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- While tourism in China has traditionally been associated with breathtaking landscapes and photo opportunities, Wang Xin (pseudonym) opted for a different kind of National Day holiday this year: watching tennis. Well before the vacation she had purchased tickets for the Jingshan Tennis Open in central China's Hubei Province. A resident of Dongguan in Guangdong Province, about 1,000 kilometers away, she first learned about Jingshan because of the tournament. "I want to watch matches featuring several young WTA (Women's Tennis Association) and ATP (Association of Tennis Professionals) players up close," said the tennis enthusiast. She planned to spend three days watching the matches and the remaining four days exploring the county-level city, taking in its scenic mountains, valleys, and forests. During this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, one of China's few annual "golden weeks," authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips, averaging 300 million a day. Data from Meituan, a major services platform, showed homestay bookings for four-to-six-night stays during the holiday rose 24 percent year on year as of Sept. 28, with county-level destinations posting particularly strong growth. Cultural and tourism authorities nationwide have introduced a range of creative initiatives to attract visitors, drawing on sports events, cultural IPs, ethnic traditions and distinctive natural landscapes. DESTINATIONS FOR DIVERSE DEMANDS Jingshan, a county-level city where tennis has been developing for more than 40 years, is known as China's "hometown of tennis." To boost tourism during the National Day holiday, local authorities announced that during the tournament period, a match ticket would entitle holders to discounts at over 100 local businesses. Merchants have also benefited from the holiday travel surge. Zuo Meng, a vendor selling knitted products, said she follows the local tennis events closely. "In Jingshan, there are tennis matches almost every week," she said, adding that a tournament can generate 6,000 to 7,000 yuan (about 895 to 1,044 U.S. dollars) in sales. Over the past two years, she has also taught knitting skills to more than 200 women so they, too, could benefit from tourism. Peng Jufang runs a farm in Wenfeng Village. Noticing tourists' enthusiasm for tennis, he founded his own tennis club in October last year. With more than 16 people coming each day to try their hand at tennis, he was kept busy during this National Day holiday, teaching visitors for over six hours a day. In 2025, Jingshan hosted 48 domestic and international sports events. The comprehensive output value of its "tennis plus" economy surpassed 3.5 billion yuan, drawing 3.52 million visits for matches and tourism. While Wang Xin enjoys tennis matches in Jingshan, cultural enthusiasts have meccas of their own to visit. Wang Yinan, in her 20s, traveled from Beijing to Ruicheng County in north China's Shanxi Province after watching the popular animation "All Wishes Come True." Hometown of the legendary figure behind the film's main protagonist, Lyu Dongbin, Ruicheng is home to the Yongle Palace, which is known for its celebrated murals. "It is such an exciting trip, and it's incredible to be in Lyu's hometown," said Wang, as she browsed creative products at the Yongle Palace store. Liu Haibo, chairman of the Yongle Cultural Tourism Investment and Construction Co., Ltd., said the scenic site rolled out customized services to sustain its tourism growth following its viral popularity. Visitors can take photos in dedicated photo zones, guides explain the murals by linking them to scenes from the film, and tourists can attend interactive classes to learn mural copying and line drawing. The movie has helped raise the profile of Ruicheng, making it a sought-after destination, especially among young people. Statistics showed that between Oct. 1 and 5, Yongle Palace received about 80,000 visits, up more than 50 percent year on year. The ancient township of Fenghuang in Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture, central China's Hunan Province, has kept its tourist momentum following the Sept. 25-27 Mid-Autumn Festival holiday. During the National Day holiday, some visitors seeking to avoid the crowds have ventured beyond the ancient town of Fenghuang into surrounding mountains and villages, exploring rich ethnic cultures, such as Miao welcoming rituals, lantern shows and folk performances. INTERNATIONAL VISITORS JOINING THE RUSH The diverse tourism resources in China's counties are also luring international visitors away from metropolises like Beijing and Shanghai and toward niche attractions. Lucas Martin, 28, from France, visited Fenghuang for the first time after touring major Chinese cities. "Fenghuang feels entirely different from big cities," he said. "You can slow down here. You can admire the distinctive stilt houses lining the Tuojiang River and observe local residents in their daily lives." The in-depth county exploration impressed him with the town's authentic living vibe. "This is not merely a tourist attraction. Walking along the river and pausing at street corners makes me feel more than just a passing sightseer." Emma Wilson, an Australian traveler who is exploring small towns and countryside across China, tried on Miao ceremonial costumes in Fenghuang. "It is magical to walk into the old streets, dressed like locals," she said. Shop staff carefully helped her get fitted in the ethnic costume. "A simple landscape photo fades quickly from memory. But putting on traditional clothing, tasting local food and learning the stories behind folk customs create experiences that stay with you far longer," she said. Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries as of September, allowing eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days. In a separate move, authorities extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. So far the number of eligible countries has increased to 57. Official data revealed that foreign nationals made nearly 61.29 million border crossings in the first eight months of 2026, up 19.5 percent year on year, while one of the leading mobile payment platforms, Weixin Pay, reported that both the value and number of e-wallet transactions made by overseas users rose by more than 80 percent during the same period. On Sept. 24, China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced plans to develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life during 2026-2030, aimed at helping foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China. FROM "CITY WALK" TO "COUNTRY WALK" Yang Han, a researcher at an institute affiliated to the travel platform Qunar, believes that county-level tourism began to accelerate around 2023-2024, as travelers increasingly sought destinations with fewer crowds, a lively atmosphere, opportunities for relaxation and immersive local experiences, as well as greater value for money. For instance, in Ruicheng of Shanxi, a set meal for one person may cost less than 20 yuan, the price of a cup of bubble tea in Beijing. Tuo Yanzheng, a professor at the College of Tourism and Service Management, Nankai University, said county areas hold rich agricultural, ecological and cultural resources with untapped consumption potential. "The key lies in turning these resource strengths into distinctive tourism products and consumption scenarios," she said. "It can not only meet people's increasingly diverse consumption demands, but also inject new vitality into the county economy." According to Sun Jiashan, a researcher at the Central Institute of Socialism, China's tourism market has evolved from "City Walk" to "Country Walk." Steadily improving transportation has made county-level destinations more accessible. By the end of 2025, China's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail. Shortly before the National Day holiday, the country opened four major high-speed railway sections, improving transport links across several regions and making travel easier for residents. The high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, with eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. In addition, Sun noted that beyond scenic spots, historical sites and natural landscapes, tourists are increasingly drawn to vibrant scenes of everyday life, such as farmers' markets and bustling streets. "This shift also places higher demands on local cultural and tourism infrastructure and services," he said. "As overseas tourists venture beyond first-tier cities into central and western regions and county-level areas, they encounter not only the outward face of China's development but also the texture of everyday social life," he said. "This helps break through cognitive filters and information barriers in Western societies and presents a real China to the world." (Video reporters: Wang Xuetao, Yue Wenwan, Yan Rui, Hu Rong and Zhang Yujie; Video editors: Yang Zeyi, Zhang Mocheng, Zheng Xin)■
